                                                      Abstract:
The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) prepared a final environmental impact
statement (EIS) for the Sabine Pass Stage 5 Expansion Project (Project), proposed by Sabine Pass Liquefaction,
LLC; Sabine Pass Liquefaction Stage V, LLC; Sabine Crossing Pipeline, LLC; and Cheniere Creole Trail
Pipeline, L.P. (collectively, the Applicants) in the above-referenced dockets. The Applicants propose to expand
the existing Sabine Pass Liquefied Natural Gas (SPLNG) Terminal facility in Cameron Parish, Louisiana by
adding three new liquefaction trains and appurtenant facilities; construct and operate the Sabine Crossing
Pipeline, a new, 48-inch-diameter, 55.6-mile-long natural gas pipeline as well as one new compressor station,
six new meter stations, and other new appurtenant facilities in Liberty, Chambers, and Jefferson Counties, Texas
and Cameron Parish, Louisiana; and construct and operate the new Tarpon Compressor Station in Cameron
Parish, Louisiana, expand the existing Gillis Compressor Station in Beauregard Parish, Louisiana, and modify
an existing delivery meter station in Cameron Parish, Louisiana, all along the existing Creole Trail Pipeline
System. Collectively, the construction of these facilities is referred to in this document as the Sabine Pass Stage
5 Expansion Project. The purpose of the Project is to expand the Applicants’ liquefied natural gas (LNG)
production capabilities to deliver up to a total of 3.6 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas to the SPLNG
Terminal facility. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Department of Transportation, U.S. Coast Guard,
the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration – National Marine Fisheries Service, and the U.S.
Department of Energy participated as cooperating agencies in the preparation of the final EIS. Commission
staff conclude that construction and operation of the proposed Project, with the mitigation measures
recommended in the final EIS, would result in some adverse environmental effects; however, effects would be
reduced to less-than-significant levels.

TO THE INTERESTED PARTY:

        The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) has prepared
a final environmental impact statement (EIS) for the Sabine Pass Stage 5 Expansion Project
(Project), proposed by Sabine Pass Liquefaction, LLC; Sabine Pass Liquefaction Stage V,
LLC; Sabine Crossing Pipeline, LLC; and Cheniere Creole Trail Pipeline, L.P.
(collectively, the Applicants) in the above-referenced dockets. 1 The Applicants propose to

expand the existing Sabine Pass Liquefied Natural Gas (SPLNG) Terminal facility in
Cameron Parish, Louisiana by adding three new liquefaction trains and appurtenant
facilities; construct and operate the Sabine Crossing Pipeline (SCPL), a new,
48-inch-diameter, 55.6-mile-long natural gas pipeline as well as one new compressor
station, six new meter stations, and other new appurtenant facilities in Liberty, Chambers,
and Jefferson Counties, Texas and Cameron Parish, Louisiana; and construct and operate
the new greenfield Tarpon Compressor Station in Cameron Parish, Louisiana, expand the
existing Gillis Compressor Station in Beauregard Parish, Louisiana, and modify an existing
delivery meter station in Cameron Parish, Louisiana, all along the existing Creole Trail
Pipeline System (CTPL).

        FERC is the lead federal agency for authorizing interstate natural gas transmission
facilities under the Natural Gas Act of 1938 (NGA) and the lead federal agency for
preparation of the final EIS. The final EIS assesses the potential environmental effects of
the construction and operation of the SPLNG Terminal Expansion, SCPL and SCPL
Aboveground Facilities, and CTPL Aboveground Facilities (collectively referred to as “the
Project”) in accordance with the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act

final EIS are to: identify and assess the potential effects on the natural and human
environment; describe and evaluate reasonable alternatives; identify and recommend
mitigation measures; and facilitate public involvement in the environmental review
process. The EIS concludes that for most resources, the construction and operation of the
Project would result in limited environmental effects. Most environmental effects would
be temporary or short-term during construction, but some long-term and permanent
environmental effects would occur in wetlands, forested lands, visual resources, and on air
quality. This determination is based on our review of the information provided by the
Applicants and further developed from environmental information requests; scoping;
literature research; consideration of potential alternatives; contacts with federal, state, and
local agencies; and other stakeholders. We conclude that effects would be less than
significant with implementation of the Applicants’ proposed avoidance, minimization, and
mitigation measures as well as the environmental and engineering conditions we
recommend the Commission include in any Project authorization it may issue. In addition,
based on a preliminary engineering and technical review of the SPLNG Terminal
Expansion design, we conclude there are acceptable layers of protection or safeguards that
would reduce the risk of a potentially hazardous scenario from developing into an event
that could impact the offsite public.

       Two districts of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Department of
Transportation, the U.S. Coast Guard, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric
Administration – National Marine Fisheries Service, and the U.S. Department of Energy
participated as cooperating agencies in the preparation of the final EIS. Cooperating
agencies have jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to resources potentially
affected by the proposal and participate in the NEPA analysis. The U.S. Army Corps of
Engineers will use the EIS to consider the issuance of Section 404 of the Clean Water Act.
Although the cooperating agencies provided input towards the conclusions and
recommendations presented in the final EIS, the agencies will present their own
conclusions and recommendations in their respective records of decision (where
applicable) for the Project.

resource agencies, elected officials, environmental groups and non-governmental

newspapers, and other stakeholders. The final EIS is only available in electronic format.
It may be viewed and downloaded from FERC’s website (www.ferc.gov), on the natural

by using the eLibrary link on FERC’s website. Click on the eLibrary link

number in the “Docket Number” field, excluding the last three digits (i.e. CP24-75,
CP25-505, or CP25-506). Be sure you have selected an appropriate date range. For
assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov or toll
free at (866) 208-3676, or for TTY, contact (202) 502-8659.

Air Quality

          The Project would result in air quality effects associated with construction, including
emissions from fossil-fueled construction equipment, marine vessels, fugitive dust, and open
burning. In general, construction activities would increase air pollutant emissions and ambient
concentrations in the vicinity of the Project at various points during the construction period. The
magnitude of the effect on air quality would vary with time due to the construction schedule
(i.e., intensity of construction activities), mobility of the sources, the variety/type of construction
equipment, and the overlap of emissions commissioning. There may be localized minor to moderate
elevated levels of fugitive dust and tailpipe emissions in the vicinity of construction areas during
periods of peak construction activity. Considering these factors, we determine that construction of
the Project would affect local air quality on an intermittent basis. However, construction emissions
would not have long-term, significant effects on air quality. Based on the temporary nature of
construction activities and the mitigation measures proposed by the Applicants, we conclude that
construction of the Project would not result in significant effects on air quality.

noise sources include heavy construction machinery, marine vessels and pile driving. With the

per day for the duration of construction. Predictive noise modeling indicates that construction of
the SPLNG Terminal Expansion would result in imperceptible increases in noise levels at the
identified noise sensitive areas. Sabine Pass would conduct noise surveys in response to
substantiated noise complaints to verify compliance with applicable noise criteria and to evaluate
whether additional mitigation measures are necessary. Noise effects due to construction of the

continuous, 24 hours a day, operations lasting 1 to 3 days. Based on the mitigation measures
proposed, the short-term nature of construction, we conclude that construction noise effects would
be temporary and less than significant.

Alternatives

        We considered and evaluated alternatives to the proposed Project, including the no-action
alternative, system alternatives, major route and aboveground facility alternatives, and minor route
variations. We evaluated potential system alternatives for the four pipelines currently supplying
natural gas to the SPLNG terminal and concluded that none have sufficient capacity to meet the
proposed export volume without additional pipeline infrastructure. Multiple alternative sites for
aboveground facilities were evaluated. Upon review of environmental and technical factors, we
concluded that the alternative site options do not provide significant environmental advantages
over the proposed sites. Three major SCPL route alternatives were evaluated and none offered
significant environmental advantages over the proposed route. For the reasons discussed above,
we conclude that the proposed Project, with our recommended mitigation measures, is the
preferred alternative to meet the Project objectives.

2.1     SPLNG TERMINAL EXPANSION

         Sabine Pass proposes to construct and operate three new liquefaction trains (Trains 7, 8, and 9,

SPLNG Terminal in Cameron Parish, Louisiana). The SPLNG Terminal is currently authorized under

Terminal Expansion would increase the number of LNG Carriers (LNGC) in the Gulf of America
and Sabine Pass Ship Channel from 580 to 740 LNGCs per year (an addition of up to 160 vessels
per year).

4.1.2 HDD and DPI Feasibility

        The HDD and DPI pipeline construction methods are described in section 2.6.4.1.
Subsurface conditions that can affect feasibility of an HDD or DPI include excessive rock strength
and abrasiveness, unconsolidated gravel and boulder materials, poor bedrock quality, solution
cavities, and artesian conditions. It is also possible for HDD and DPI pipeline installations to fail,
primarily from encountering unexpected geologic conditions such as transitions from coarse
unconsolidated materials into bedrock or if the pipe were to become lodged in the hole during
pullback.

        During HDD and DPI activities, drilling fluid consisting primarily of water and bentonite
clay is pumped under pressure through the inside of the drill pipe and flows back (returns) to the
drill entry point along an annular space between the outside of the drill pipe and the drilled hole.
In certain conditions the drilling fluid can seep into the surrounding rocks and sediment. Drilling
fluid losses typically occur when the drilling fluid flows through the porous spaces in the soil
through which the HDD or DPI profile passes or within fractures contained in the rock formation.

4.1.4.1 Seismicity and Soil Liquefaction

        Seismic hazards include earthquakes, ground faulting, and secondary effects such as soil
liquefaction. Traditionally, peak ground acceleration (PGA), expressed as a percentage of the
acceleration of gravity, is used to quantify these ground motion from earthquakes. Project
components are in areas with a less than 1 percent chance of minor-damage ground shaking from
an earthquake.

        There are no known active Quaternary faults within the vicinity of the Project facilities,
but a regional system of normal faults do exist within the Gulf Coast Basin, and several have been
identified in the general vicinity of the SPLNG Terminal Expansion (Stevenson & McCulloh,
2001; McCulloh & Heinrich, 2012). However, due to the long-term stability over the past
23 million years or more (Wong et al., 2023), there is minimal probability of seismic-induced
movement along growth faults. These faults exhibit less than 0.2 millimeters of movement per
year (USGS, 2025b) and are not typically associated with earthquakes because the sediments are
unable to support the stresses required for the propagation of signiﬁcant seismic ruptures that could
cause damaging ground motions (Wheeler and Heinrich, 1998). Therefore, we do not expect
seismicity to affect the Project.

        Soil liquefaction may occur when loose, cohesionless, and water-saturated soils are
exposed to ground shaking due to an earthquake. The phenomenon is most often observed in
loose, low-density sandy soils subject to high water tables, or those deposits laid down in a fluvial
environment. The Project is underlain primarily by clay soils that are not susceptible to
liquefaction. The Tarpon Compressor Station and CTPL Delivery Meter Station are underlain by
aquents and udifluvents soils, both of which are alluvial with low clay content making the area
potentially susceptible to soil liquefaction. However, based on the low seismic hazard, this risk is
low. As a result, we do not expect liquefaction to significantly affect the Project.

slopes, and shallow debris flows. The USGS Landslide Overview Map of the Conterminous
United States shows general delineations where large numbers of landslides have occurred and
areas which are susceptible to landsliding. The landslide incidence and susceptibility are rated low
within the SPLNG Terminal, SPLNG Terminal Expansion and SCPL areas (Radbruch-Hall et al.,
1982). In the areas of the CTPL Aboveground Facilities, there is a very low landslide potential
(Mirus et al., 2024). The topography in the existing Project area is generally flat to gently level,
with steeper areas of sloping at earthworks (e.g., berms) and riverbanks. The Applicants would

activities in accordance with applicable federal and state requirements. The CTPL Delivery Meter
Station would be constructed on land that has been leveled and graded and the Tarpon Compressor

diminished, soils may have a greater erosion potential, and natural drainage patterns may be
modified, which is of particular concern in agricultural and hydric soils. The susceptibility of soils
to compaction varies based on moisture content, composition, grain size, and density of the soil.

 4.2.1.4 Low Revegetation Potential

        Soils that have low revegetation potential are considered areas of revegetation concern.
Soils with poor revegetation potential may need additional management and may be difficult to
revegetate, which can lead to increased erosion, reduction in wildlife habitat, and adverse visual
effects. The land capability classification is a system of grouping soils primarily based on
capability to produce common cultivated crops and pasture plants without deteriorating over a long
period of time (NRCS, 2017).

        The Applicants would promote revegetation through the implementation of measures from
the Plan and Procedures, including but not limited selecting and applying appropriate seed mixes
and fertilizer as recommended; seeding permanent vegetation within recommended seeding dates;
preparing the seedbed in disturbed areas up to 3 to 4 inches deep using appropriate equipment;
implementing temporary stabilization measures (e.g., using mulch in upland areas); and follow-up
monitoring after the first growing season, and if necessary, the second growing season to determine
success of revegetation. Upland soils disturbed by the Project would be revegetated using seed
mixes based on recommendations approved and specified by local soil conservationists and/or land
management agencies or landowner agreements. The restoration of affected lands is a process and
may be accomplished relatively quickly (1 to 2 growing seasons) or may require several years to
complete, depending on several factors. Restoration of affected lands can be adversely affected
by weather conditions such as drought or abnormal rainfall, landowner actions (e.g., physical
changes to land use, cattle grazing), and/or third-party actions including non-Project use/activities.
It is our expectation that if initial restoration activities are unsuccessful, the Applicants, in
consultation with the affected landowner and consistent with our environmental compliance
monitoring and reporting requirements, would continue to assess, take action, and implement
measures to ensure the eventual restoration of the affected resources.

Florida and generally yields large amounts of water for public, agricultural, and industrial needs.

sources should the aquifer become contaminated. The Project facilities would overlie the local

4.4.4.1 Essential Fish Habitat

       EFH represents areas of high economic importance due to the dependence on recreational
and commercial fisheries directly and indirectly associated with these areas and includes tidally
influenced waters (estuarine water column and benthic areas) and tidally influenced marsh, which
is generally east and southeast of milepost 46 within the Project area. The Gulf Council has
designated EFH for adults and juveniles of 15 species of finfish and shellfish within the Sabine
Lake estuary. A review of the Gulf Council EFH Portal and correspondence received on
October 24, 2023 (NOAA-NMFS, 2023b) from NOAA-NMFS found that five species may be
present within estuaries and adjacent wetlands within the Project area and potentially affected by
the construction of the SPLNG Terminal Expansion, SCPL, and SCPL Aboveground Facilities.
